title: Explicit implementation and boxing
sub: Interface-only methods, a struct in a box and calls through a stub
cards/0/body:
A class implements an interface method in one of two ways.

Implicitly — an ordinary public method with the same name and signature. It is visible both through the class and through the interface.

Explicitly — the name is prefixed with the interface and there is no access modifier. You cannot call such a method through a class variable, only through an interface reference.
cards/0/deep:
In IL an implicit implementation is a public method flagged virtual final newslot. The compiler makes it virtual so it gets a slot in the method table, and seals it unless you wrote virtual yourself.

An explicit implementation is a private method named System.IDisposable.Dispose with an .override directive (a MethodImpl record) that binds it to the interface method. You cannot write a dotted name in C#, so it never clashes with ordinary methods.

An explicit implementation cannot be virtual or abstract. If a derived class needs to change the behavior, the explicit method simply calls a protected virtual one — that is how the classic Dispose pattern works.
cards/1/q: Report implements IExportable.Export() explicitly. Which line does not compile?
cards/1/explain: An explicitly implemented method is not among the public members of the class. Through a variable of type Report it is invisible — error CS1061. Through the interface (a variable or a cast) it is fine.
cards/2/body:
Three typical reasons:

  • A name clash. Two interfaces require a method with the same signature but different meaning. Explicit implementation gives each its own code.
  • An old untyped method. IEnumerable<T> inherits the non-generic IEnumerable. The generic GetEnumerator is made public, and the one returning plain IEnumerator is made explicit so it stays out of the way.
  • A member nobody needs day to day. List<T> implements ICollection<T>.IsReadOnly explicitly: for a list it is always false and would only be noise in IntelliSense.
cards/3/q: A class implements IPrinter and IPlotter, and both require void Print(). Through IPrinter it must print text, through IPlotter it must draw a chart. How?
cards/3/options/0: Implement at least one of the methods explicitly
cards/3/options/1: Write two public Print() methods in one class
cards/3/options/2: You cannot: these interfaces are incompatible in one class
cards/3/options/3: Mark one of the methods with new
cards/3/explain: A single public Print() would satisfy both interfaces at once, but with one behavior. An explicit void IPlotter.Print() gives the second interface its own code, while the public Print() stays for IPrinter and for calls through the class.
cards/3/wrong/1: Two methods with the same signature in one class is error CS0111.
cards/3/wrong/2: They are compatible: identical signatures in different interfaces are common, and explicit implementation exists for exactly that.
cards/4/title: Explicit implementation on a struct: only through a box
cards/4/body:
As in the "Value types all the way" unit: an interface is a reference type, and a struct converted to it is boxed. A method called through the interface changes the box, not the original variable.

Explicit implementation makes this trap mandatory. On a class the explicit method is merely hidden, but on a struct there is no ordinary call path left at all: c.Inc() does not compile, and ((ICounter)c).Inc() creates a box, increments it and throws it away at once. The change is lost silently.
cards/4/deep:
In IL a call through the interface is box followed by callvirt on the interface method. The box is a full object with a header and a type pointer: for Counter on x64 that is 24 bytes.

That is why explicit implementation is avoided on mutable structs. In the libraries it shows up on struct enumerators: List<T>.Enumerator explicitly implements IEnumerator.Current (returning object) and IEnumerator.Reset. Nobody uses them through the public API, and foreach over a List<T> itself calls the public MoveNext and Current directly, without a box.
cards/5/q: Counter from the previous card: Inc is implemented explicitly. What does this print?
cards/5/explain: The first cast creates a box, increments it and throws it away: c.Value stays 0. ICounter a = c boxes c again, still with zero, and a.Inc() brings that box to 1.
cards/5/wrong/1: That would be true if ((ICounter)c).Inc() changed the variable c itself. But the cast works on a copy.
cards/5/wrong/3: Box a was created from c, and c still holds 0: the first box is already gone.
cards/6/title: The box-free path: a constrained generic
cards/6/body:
There is a way to call a struct's explicit method without boxing: a generic constrained with where T : ICounter. For a value-type T the JIT compiles a separate copy of the method, knows the exact type and calls the implementation directly — an explicit one too, since an explicit implementation is an ordinary method, just private.

For the change to reach the caller, pass the parameter by ref. Without it the method works on its own copy of the struct: no box, but nothing changes outside either.
cards/6/deep:
For x.Inc() inside a generic the compiler emits the constrained. prefix:

ldarg.0
constrained. !!T
callvirt instance void ICounter::Inc()

For a value-type T that implements the interface method itself — implicitly or explicitly — the runtime finds the implementation in the struct type and calls it through the managed pointer, without a box. The explicit method being private does not get in the way: access is checked against the interface method, not the implementation. The compiler uses the same trick in using and foreach with a struct: Dispose on a struct enumerator is called without boxing, even if it is implemented explicitly.
cards/7/q: Complete the method: it must increment any struct counter without boxing, and the change must be visible outside
cards/7/explain: ref gives the method access to the caller's variable itself. The ICounter constraint allows calling Inc and lets the JIT make a direct call without a box. With in, Inc would run on a defensive copy and the changes would be lost; with class you could not pass a struct at all.
cards/8/title: How the CLR finds an interface method
cards/8/body:
For a class's virtual method the slot number in the method table is known in advance: in a derived class the overridden ToString sits where the base one does. The call is a couple of memory reads and an indirect jump.

That does not work for interfaces. A class implements any number of interfaces, and the same method ICounter.Inc ends up in different slots in different classes. So CoreCLR calls an interface method through a stub with a cache: the call site remembers the type it has seen, and while objects of that type keep arriving, the call is almost as fast as a virtual one.

It gets more expensive where many different types pass through one call site: then the implementation is looked up in a shared hash table.
cards/8/deep:
The mechanism is called virtual stub dispatch (VSD). The call site goes through an indirection cell, and the runtime rewrites it as it learns more:

  • lookup stub — the first call: passes the method token and the object type to a shared resolver;
  • dispatch stub — afterwards: compares the object's MethodTable with the remembered one and jumps straight to the implementation, falling through to the resolve stub on a mismatch;
  • resolve stub — if misses pile up, the call site is treated as polymorphic and switched here: a lookup of the "token + type" pair in a global cache.

On top of that, the JIT with dynamic PGO (on by default since .NET 8) does guarded devirtualization: if the profile shows one class almost always arrives, the JIT inserts a type check and a direct — and therefore inlinable — call, keeping the stub as the fallback. Native AOT uses its own caching scheme without VSD. The details change between versions, so measure the cost of a specific call site.
cards/9/q: Why can an interface method not be called like a virtual one — by a slot number known in advance?
cards/9/options/0: The same interface method sits in different slots in different classes
cards/9/options/1: Interface methods do not go into the class's method table
cards/9/options/2: Structs implement interfaces too, and they have no method table
cards/9/options/3: Interface slots are reassigned on every garbage collection
cards/9/explain: Virtual method slots are inherited down the class chain, so an override keeps the same number. Each class has its own set of interfaces, and there is no common number for ICounter.Inc — it is looked up by the object's type and the result is cached in the stub.
cards/9/wrong/1: They do: an implicit implementation is a virtual final method with its own slot. The point is that the slot number differs between classes.
cards/10/q: Counter is a struct implementing ICounter; c is a Counter variable; list is a List<int>. Where does boxing happen by the rules of the language and IL? Select all.
cards/10/options/2: Bump(ref c), where Bump<T>(ref T x) where T : ICounter
cards/10/explain: Assigning to an interface boxes the struct. Iterating through IEnumerable<int> gets List<int>.Enumerator through the interface — boxed as well. The constrained generic, reading a property of the struct and foreach over the List<int> itself manage without one.
cards/11/q: Match the construct to what it means
cards/11/pairs/0/1: Explicit implementation: call only through the interface
cards/11/pairs/2/1: A call without a box for a value-type T
cards/11/pairs/3/1: IL prefix before callvirt in a generic
cards/11/pairs/4/1: Checks the object type against the remembered one
